steps.action:
# The Light at Morrow Point

The fog came in the way it always did — not all at once, but in suggestions. First a softening of the horizon, then the erasure of the distant tree line on the mainland shore, then finally the world reduced to a circle of gray water no wider than a stone's throw, with the lighthouse standing at its center like the last nail in a disappearing world.

Elara Voss had kept the light at Morrow Point for eleven years.

She had come here the way most people came to isolated places — running from something she couldn't name clearly enough to outrun it any other way. A marriage that had gone quiet in the particular way that is worse than arguing. A city apartment that had begun to feel like a display case in which she was both the curator and the exhibit. A career in marine biology that had somehow drifted, like everything else, into the management of paperwork rather than the study of living things.

The Coast Guard posting had been a joke at first — something her colleague Marcus had shown her on a Tuesday afternoon when the office felt particularly airless. *Lighthouse Keeper, Morrow Point Station. Remote posting. Must be comfortable with extended solitude. Knowledge of basic electrical systems preferred.*

"Can you imagine?" Marcus had said, laughing into his coffee.

She had applied the next morning.

---

The lighthouse was not romantic in the way that lighthouses are in paintings. The paintings always get the light wrong — they show it as warm and golden, the color of hearth fires and welcome. The actual light was clinical, almost aggressive, a rotating beam engineered not for comfort but for visibility at distance. Up close, in the lantern room, it was loud in a way that surprised most visitors. The mechanism clicked and hummed. The Fresnel lens, all those concentric glass rings, gathered and focused light with a kind of ruthless efficiency that Elara found beautiful for precisely that reason. It did not pretend. It did not gesture. It simply performed its function with complete commitment, over and over, every night, for no audience except the dark.

She had learned to love the machinery the way you love a reliable friend. She maintained it obsessively — not out of anxiety, though the consequences of failure were real enough, but out of genuine affection. She oiled the rotation gears on a schedule. She tested the backup generators with a thoroughness that exceeded the official requirements. She kept records in a logbook using a system she had developed herself, more detailed than the standard form demanded.

The Coast Guard inspector who visited each spring, a tired man named Beaumont who smelled of diesel and antacid tablets, had once told her she was the most conscientious keeper he'd encountered in thirty years of inspections.

"I don't have much else to do," she had said, which was both true and not the whole truth.

---

The whole truth was more complicated and took her years to understand.

In the city, she had been surrounded by people and had felt profoundly, almost medically, alone. Out here, alone in any objective sense, she rarely felt loneliness. She had theories about this. She thought it had something to do with honesty — the island didn't pretend to be something other than what it was, and this freed her to stop pretending too. She was a woman who needed quiet. She was a woman who thought better when the thinking wasn't interrupted every eleven minutes. She was a woman who found the turning of a lighthouse beam more companionable than most conversation.

She also had the radio, the monthly supply boat, and occasional visits from the families of fishermen who wanted to picnic on the island's small patch of grass on summer Sundays. She was not a hermit. She simply had learned, eleven years in, what the correct dosage of other people was for her particular constitution.

Her ex-husband, David, had said once — not cruelly, just observationally — that she was like a tide pool. Beautiful and full of life, but only at certain times, and you had to know when to look, and you absolutely could not touch.

She had been hurt by this. Now she thought he was essentially right, and that there was nothing wrong with being a tide pool.

---

On the night of the worst storm of her tenure — a November gale that the weather service had underestimated by a factor that would later cause a formal review — Elara was in the lantern room when she saw the distress flare.

It went up to the southeast, weak through the rain, orange-red and dissolving almost immediately into the dark. She almost missed it. She had been watching the light's rotation as she sometimes did, in a state of mind she could only describe as active meditation, and the flare appeared in the corner of her vision like a word glimpsed on a page you weren't reading.

She pressed her face to the glass, cupping her hands around her eyes. The rain hit the lantern room windows horizontally. Below, the sea was doing what the sea does in a serious gale — building waves that were architectural in their scale and intention, structures that assembled themselves from the chaos with terrible deliberateness before collapsing again into chaos.

Another flare. Same direction. Perhaps a quarter mile out, perhaps more — distance was nearly impossible to judge in these conditions.

She was on the radio before the second flare had faded, calling in coordinates, giving conditions, giving her assessment, which was that conditions were extremely dangerous and that whatever was out there was in serious trouble. The Coast Guard station on the mainland confirmed receipt and told her rescue assets were being dispatched, ETA uncertain given the weather.

Uncertain. In these conditions, uncertain meant a long time. A long time was something a quarter mile offshore, in this sea, in November, might not have.

She thought about this for approximately forty-five seconds.

Then she went down to the equipment room and began pulling out the gear she needed.

---

There are things that look like courage from the outside that feel, from the inside, like simple arithmetic. Elara had run the calculation: a person or persons in the water, in the dark, in November, with wave heights that would swamp the island's small rescue skiff, but also with the skiff as the only available option, and with her as the only available person, and with the time until Coast Guard arrival a variable that tilted the equation in a direction that only had one response.

She was not brave. She was just good at math.

The skiff was small and old and had a tendency to yaw to port that she had reported in three consecutive annual maintenance requests that had been acknowledged and not addressed. She compensated for the yaw the way she compensated for all the lighthouse's idiosyncrasies — automatically, without resentment, because this was the equipment she had.

The waves were worse than they had looked from above. Up in the lantern room, you had perspective, and perspective imposes a kind of order on things. Down on the water, there was no order. There was only the next wave, and the angle at which you needed to meet it, and the controlled application of throttle, and then the next wave.

She found them twenty minutes later — two men, a father and his adult son, she would learn afterward, whose fishing boat had broken up on a submerged rock that appeared on no chart because it was a rock that had migrated, over decades, from deeper water, creeping shoreward through a process that the son, who turned out to have a graduate degree in geology, would later explain to her in a letter she received that spring.

The father had a broken arm. The son was hypothermic but functional. Getting them into the skiff was the hardest physical labor of her life, harder than anything she had imagined, and she had imagined it fairly specifically on the way out.

She got them in.

She got them back.

---

The news coverage lasted a week. A reporter from the mainland came out on the supply boat and took photographs of her standing outside the lighthouse, squinting into the light in the way you squint when someone points a camera at you against a bright sky. The headline used the word "heroine," which she found both embarrassing and faintly inaccurate. The Coast Guard gave her a commendation. Beaumont, the inspector, sent a card.

The father — his name was Gerald — sent a letter too, written in a careful, slightly formal hand that suggested a man who did not write many letters but took the ones he wrote seriously. He thanked her. He said he did not have the right words. He said she had given him back his son, which was the greatest gift one person could give another. He said if she ever needed anything, ever, she only had to ask.

She wrote back. She thanked him for his letter. She said she was glad they were safe. She said the light at Morrow Point was visible on clear nights at a distance of twenty-two miles, and that she would keep it burning.

She did not tell him — because it was too private, or too strange, or too close to something she didn't have words for herself yet — that the night after the rescue, she had gone up to the lantern room and sat beside the turning light for three hours, not doing anything in particular. Just watching the beam go around. Feeling, perhaps for the first time in her life, that she was precisely where she was supposed to be, doing precisely what she was supposed to do, and that this was not a small thing.

That it was, in fact, everything.

---

The fog comes in again tonight. Elara climbs the hundred and twelve steps — she has never lost count; she wonders sometimes if she will count them on her deathbed, silently, out of habit — and settles into the lantern room. The light is already running. The light is always already running. It doesn't wait for her, which is one of the things she loves about it.

She opens her logbook. She writes the date, the weather conditions, the sea state, the visibility. She writes these things with the same care she has always used, a care that is neither compulsive nor performative but simply proportionate. This is what the moment requires. She provides it.

Outside, somewhere in the gray, a ship is finding its way. She doesn't know which ship. She doesn't need to. The light goes out, turns, comes back — out, turns, comes back — patient and indifferent and absolutely reliable, the same message it has always sent, the only message a lighthouse knows how to send:

*Here. Here. Here. Here.*

And she tends it. And the fog holds the island. And the island holds the light. And the light holds the dark at the distance required.

And that is enough. That is exactly enough.
